title: RSI2: Five In, Zero Through. The Later Prices Stayed Locked.

voice_performance.performance_intent: A calm lab walkthrough for one beginner; exact results are stated without turning them into a promise.
voice_performance.energy_curve: Open with the stopped SPY lane, slow down for the operator inequalities, then separate the Dow contrast and close on unanswered execution questions.
voice_performance.pause_policy: Pause after every exact number and at every evidence-boundary change.

sections.label: The stock branch stops before the chamber
sections.text: The SPY RSI2 screen stopped five candidates before the later prices opened. We have a daily window from 1996-07-12 through 2011-05-26. Five versions enter, and all fail. The next phase has zero. There is no holdout return for SPY, and no later result. That can look like a dead end, but it is the result. We can look at the data and see what stopped the list. Then we will look at the Dow futures on its own. Keep the two paths separate. SPY stops at intake. The Dow reaches the later test. You can look at the data and see the result.

sections.label: Freeze before the later block
sections.text: You know how a later test can go wrong. You look at the result, and then make a change. You look again. Freeze the version before you open that door. Out-of-sample means the later prices did not help you choose it. A holdout is the later part kept shut while you choose. Pick first, write it down, and open the door once. If you use the result to make another choice, those prices now join the choice. Now the question changes. SPY has five rows, and none go forward. The Dow has a later group. Choose the version first, then look at the later prices.

sections.label: The vocabulary of a sealed test
sections.text: Let us slow down and name these words. You know, in-sample is the part we use to choose. Out-of-sample is the part we save for later. The first part gives us a way to build the rule, and the second part lets us see what happens with new prices. Overfitting is when the rule follows the old path too closely. Curve-fitting is the same problem when we move the settings. If you try enough settings, you will find something that looks good, but that does not mean it will work again. Frozen parameters are the numbers we leave alone. A segmented backtest has fixed blocks with separate jobs. Walk-forward moves the start and does it again. In this run, we have one first part and one later part. That gives us context; this run has no walk-forward result. Warmup bars are the history an indicator needs before we use its value. We keep them outside the trade-result count. That is a method rule; it adds no new SPY result.
sections.speaker_directions: Calm, precise beginner teaching; pause after exact numbers and before the boundary.

sections.label: Read the gate as inequalities
sections.text: Here is the row, and here is the arithmetic. Profit factor is 0.806004. The target is more than 1.3. Return over drawdown is -0.420205. The target is more than 4. Trades per month is 0.392308. The target is more than 2 trades per month. Write each check down: 0.806004 > 1.3 is false. -0.420205 > 4 is false. 0.392308 trades per month > 2 trades per month is false. Profit factor is a unitless ratio: gross winning dollars divided by gross losing dollars. Return over drawdown is a unitless ratio: net result divided by the largest measured drawdown. Trades per month is a rate, with units of trades per month.

sections.label: Five rows stay five rows

sections.label: Why selection pressure matters
sections.text: Why does this matter? You know, the problem starts when the development history feels too familiar. You look at the old prices, try many rules, and keep the one that looks good. Then you start to learn the path instead of testing the idea. Curve-fitting can mean moving one threshold, one exit, or one window after you see the result. White's data-snooping paper warns that a result can show up by chance when the same data chooses and judges the rule. Trading-rule research gives us the same warning. The simple answer is to choose the plan first. Freeze the settings. Open the later block once. Record what happened. SPY shows the first stop. Dow shows why the later step matters.
